div.head: Chapter 12
div.p: The first entry or foothold by which the Spaniards entered the Indies and each province, kingdom, and part of them, from the time of their discovery in the year 1492 until today inclusive, as we are in December of the year 1563, was violent, abominable, tyrannical, and most cruel, and worthy of cruel enemies; and such that no people, however barbarous and lawless and irrational, could have done worse. Likewise, the course and disorder of the governance they imposed throughout that world.

The first part of this principle can be proved in a thousand ways, but to be brief we will prove it by this one. For in the said entry, that first entrance, they never observed but rather violated the order of natural and divine law, and also human law. This will be apparent by calling to mind the elements contained in the said order of the aforesaid natural, human, and divine law. The first is that, since the sole and final cause of their navigation through those seas and entry into those foreign kingdoms could not be and was no other than the preaching of the faith and the conversion of those peoples, the natural and divine order required that the very first thing done on our part and offered to those peoples should be peace. This first part is proved by Saint Matthew, chapter 10 and by Saint Luke and Saint Mark, where Christ laid down the precept that the first thing Christians going to convert unbelievers should use, was peace: "Entering the house, greet it, saying: peace be to this house, etc." The preaching of the faith and the conversion of peoples presupposes peace. For, as a certain Extravagant in omnibus, title de usuris, says: "We know and gather from the evidence of the fact that good worship is offered to the author of peace only in time of peace." And thus the first foothold and first entry of the Spaniards into the Indies ought to have been peaceable.

The second part of the order of natural and divine law: that that entry be slow and unhurried, little by little and with great caution, so that the kings and peoples of those towns would not be alarmed at seeing such unfamiliar people, bearded and fierce in appearance; for all new and unaccustomed things by their nature cause alarm, seeming greater evils than they are and less remediable, as Saint Augustine says in book 2 of the Confessions. And this is well proved by the law observare antequam, ff. De officio proconsulis, which commands that when someone is appointed as an assistant or governor to some province or city, he should first give notice to the citizens that he is coming, and win their goodwill by signifying to them that he comes for their benefit and to do them good, etc. And the reason of the law, it itself declares: "For uncertain and unexpected things often alarm the provincials and impede the acts of entry, etc."

The third, the order of natural and divine law requires, in this most supreme matter, that that entry and first entrance into each province be harmless and blameless; that is to say, that the Spaniards sent should not fall upon the natural kings and their peoples. For if it were against their will, and especially if the entry were expressly forbidden to them by deeds or by words, then it would be harmful, blameworthy, and injurious; and those kings and peoples would justly have cause to be alarmed and enraged against the Spaniards and to make war upon them and punish them as their own subjects, or more precisely, as enemies. Any prudent king or lord may freely, by the authority of natural and divine and even human law, forbid entry into his kingdom to whatever foreign persons are unknown to him, on the presumption that they do not come with the intention of probing the weaknesses and secrets of the land in order to usurp it afterwards. And this prohibition is amply proved by what Joseph said to his brothers, though it was to afflict them, yet with reasonable pretext: "You are spies," he said, "you have come to see the weak points of the land, by the life of Pharaoh, etc." Genesis 42. And the counselors of King Ammon gave this same reason, suspecting that David, being a man of war, had sent the messengers to console Hanun over his father's death under that pretext to reconnoiter the places most suitable for attacking him with war; they said to the king: "Perhaps you think David has sent consolers to you out of honor for your father; do you not see that his servants have come to you to explore, investigate, and spy out your land?" 1 Chronicles 19. This is likewise proved by the L. mercatores, Codex, De commerciis et mercatoribus; and in L. ut vim, ff. De iustitia et iure.

The fourth, the order of natural and divine law requires, and this above all: that the Spaniards whom our king and lord should send with the preachers of the faith, since they had no other legitimate cause for going to those foreign lands belonging to those peoples, should live as Christians, and that their conversation and example should be such that those unbelievers, seeing it, might be moved and encouraged to profess the Christian religion by receiving the faith and baptism, and might praise God for having sent them such people to convert them. This is proved by that passage of Matthew 5: "So let your light shine, that is, your life, before men, that they may see your works and glorify your Father who is in heaven."

And 1 Peter: "Having your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that in the very thing in which they speak against you as evildoers, seeing your good works they may glorify God on the day of visitation, that is, when God visits the unbelievers by sending them preachers of the faith."

Saint John Chrysostom, on the said words of Saint Matthew, says: "By those who teach and act, God is glorified. By those who teach and do not act, he is blasphemed. If they teach well and the Gentiles see that they act accordingly, the Gentiles who see it say: 'Blessed be God who has such servants; truly their God is the true God. For if he were not himself just, he would never hold his people so firmly to justice; for the discipline of the lord is shown by the conduct of his household.' But if they teach well and live badly, those who see them say: 'What kind of a God is theirs, who lets them do such things? Would he tolerate them doing so if he did not consent to their works? etc.'" And on 1 Timothy 3, after many most beautiful things, the same Chrysostom says: "Certainly no one would still be a pagan if we ourselves took care to be Christians as we ought and obeyed the commands and teachings of God," and a little further on: "There would be no one so fierce a beast as not to run at once to the worship of the true religion if he saw everyone practicing it." Chrysostom.

The fifth, the order of natural and divine law requires: that the Spaniards, in each province they came to on behalf of the king of Castile, after having entered with the goodwill of the kings and peoples, as has been said, should set forth and declare to them the final cause of their coming to those lands; that is to say, to bring them knowledge of the one true God, Creator and Lord of all the worlds, etc. Which ought to be given very slowly and at their own pace, modestly, gently, and quietly, and with all the other circumstances required for any good work to be good. This is proved by the second and third reasons. For if it were not done thus, such an entry would not be free of suspicion, and the kings and their peoples would be alarmed and scandalized, and consequently the harms and evils that followed from it would be imputed to the Spaniards, etc. And in particular, even without any notification, a very long span of time is required, because first they would have to learn the languages so that both sides could understand each other, without which nothing done would be worth anything in law, ut L. 1, fin., ff., De verborum significatione, cum ibi nota et alibi.
